author: fomightez
body:
I think this would allow more people hesitant about dealing with Python on their local machine use your script easily. The computational power needed to do this is not much and so the low powered, ephemeral sessions offered by the [MyBinder.org](https://mybinder.org/) system are a good fit.

Feel free to not pull this, yet simply follow [my fork of your repo](https://github.com/fomightez/PDBrenum) as a guide to what is necessary to add MyBinder launches to your own repo. Most of the additional items needed are in the `binder` directory I added.  
The launch badges I made in the README can be easily have the URL changed to point at your repo by copying the block or editing the end after your pull. Or you can generate your own custom launch badges [here](https://mybinder.readthedocs.io/en/latest/howto/badges.html). And the [MyBinder.org  main page](https://mybinder.org/) offers the standard `launch binder` badges as well. (The standard ones may be less familiar though to biologists, and so I prefer the custom ones.)

If you do pull the README, you'll want to remove the note I made under 'Attributions' trying to be clear that I simply was trying to binderize your awesome work. Or edit it back as you see fit. I expanded it.

I added a demo Jupyter notebook targeted at biologists and folks maybe unfamiliar with Jupyter.  I placed it in root to make the directory hierarchy somewhat less forboding to biologists. This is simply a suggestion but it is nice to get people up and running more quickly in a Binder session. And let's them see how to plug in what they want to accomplish easily.

I think [the issues that came up & were worked out](https://twitter.com/RolandDunbrack/status/1412987509995356161) reveal, that Binderizing is helpful on a number of levels.  

Plus, it makes easy to check with newer Python and dependencies which I now have done by making a branch of my fork, called [unpinned](https://github.com/fomightez/PDBrenum/tree/unpinned), where I remove `runtime.txt` and unpin the versions of the packages listed in `requirements.txt`. That version can be launched as a session using `https://mybinder.org/v2/gh/fomightez/PDBrenum/unpinned?filepath=demo.ipynb`. So far it works the same as best I can tell with with Python 3.7 (current version Binder uses by default) and unpinned packages. And with Python version 3.8 specified and unpinned packages (can be run via `https://mybinder.org/v2/gh/fomightez/PDBrenum/3pt8?filepath=demo.ipynb` off the 3pt8 branch I also made).

A further suggestion that I didn't address in my fork, it probably would be good to add a license.

This PR adds an extra check to the `pathToFsPath` function to check that `uri.path` is indeed a string.

We do this because CodeQL believes there is currently type confusion through parameter tampering earlier up in the codebase where this is used. See security warning [here](https://github.com/cdr/code-server/security/code-scanning/51?query=ref%3Arefs%2Fheads%2Fmain).

Fixes #3750

author: juuxel
body:
Fixes #56, fixes #250 and fixes #403.

- `flatDir` dependencies are fixed by replacing their empty group and version strings with `unspecified`
- `files`/`fileTree` dependencies (`FileCollectionDependency` instances) are fixed by adding custom logic as they aren't caught by `sourceConfig.getResolvedConfiguration().getResolvedArtifacts()`.
  - They don't go through resolution at all, and this is also why `DependencyProcessor` has custom logic for `SelfResolvingDependency`s like them. (I didn't use `SelfResolvingDependency` here because project dependencies are also instances of it, and they are already caught earlier since they are resolved properly. This would duplicate them.)

author: dmitrygx
body:
## What

Remove trying next CM callback upon destroying EP.

## Why ?

Trying next CM callback should be removed upon destroying EP to avoid calling it when UCP EP is already destroyed.

## How ?

1. Added `UCP_EP_FLAG_TRY_NEXT_CM` flag to check whether trying next CM callback scheduled or not - needed for DEBUG-only purposes and for GTESTs.
2. Introduced two GTESTs which fail wireup procedure when client is scheduling trying next CM callback.
3. Introduced filter function to remove trying next CM callback from cbq.
4. Use the new filter to remove trying next CM callback from cbq upon destroying UCP EP.
5. Destroy next UCT EP by using discarding functionality to allow calling it from async functions, e.g. UCT CM callback (resolve_cb, connect_cb).
6. Move destroying next UCT EP of CM lane to the place where scheduling trying next CM callback in order to make sure no lanes at all when doing `ucp_ep_close_nbx()` which disccards lanes in case of FORCE. So, discard shouldn't be added to progress and callbacks should be removed.

author: github-learning-lab[bot]
body:
# Welcome to the course!

We'll learn how to create a workflow that enables Continuous Delivery. You'll:
- create a workflow to deploy to staging based on a label
- create a workflow to deploy to production based on merging to main

Before you start, you should be familiar with GitHub and Continuous Integration. If you aren't sure where to start, you may want to check out these two Learning Lab courses:

- [Introduction to GitHub](https://lab.github.com/githubtraining/introduction-to-github)
- [Continuous Integration with GitHub Actions](https://lab.github.com/githubtraining/github-actions:-continuous-integration/)

### What is Continuous Delivery?

[Martin Fowler](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ContinuousDelivery.html) defined Continuous Delivery very simply in a 2013 post as follows:

> Continuous Delivery is a software development discipline where you build software in such a way that the software can be released to production at any time.

A lot of things go into delivering "continuously". These things can range from culture and behavior to specific automation. In this course, we're going to focus on deployment automation.

### Setting up environments and kicking off deployments

Automation works at its best when a set of triggers work harmoniously to set up and deploy to target environments. Engineers at many companies, like at GitHub, typically use a ChatOps command as a trigger. The trigger itself isn't incredibly important.

In our use case, we'll use labels as triggers for multiple tasks:
- When someone applies a "spin up environment" label to a pull request, that'll tell GitHub Actions that we'd like to set up our resources on an Azure environment.
- When someone applies a "stage" label to a pull request, that'll be our indicator that we'd like to deploy our application to a staging environment.
- When someone applies a "destroy environment" label to a pull request, we'll tear down any resources that are running on our Azure account.

For now, we'll focus on staging. We'll spin up and destroy our environment in a later step.

## Step 1: Configure a trigger based on labels

In a GitHub Actions workflow, the `on` step defines what causes the workflow to run. In this case, we want the workflow to run whenever a label is applied to the pull request.

### :keyboard: Activity: Configure the workflow trigger based on a label being added

1. Edit the `deploy-staging.yml` file on this branch, or [use this quick link](https://github.com/farahsameen/github-actions-continuous-delivery-azure/edit/staging-workflow/.github/CHANGETHIS/deploy-staging.yml?) _(We recommend opening the quick link in another tab)_
2. Change the name of the directory `CHANGETHIS` to `workflows`, so the title of this file with the path is `.github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml`. If you're working on the GitHub.com user interface, see the suggestion below for how to rename.
3. Edit the contents of this file to trigger a job called `build` on a label

<details><summary>Changing the name of a directory</summary>

If you're working locally, rename your file or drag-and-drop the file into the proper directory as you'd normally do. If you're working on GitHub.com, you can change the name of a directory by changing its filename and using the Backspace key until you reach the directory, as follows:
1. In the file name field, click in front of the first character in the file name
1. Press <kbd>Backspace</kbd> or <kbd>Delete</kbd> on your keyboard until you see the path you want to keep. You can continue to press <kbd>Backspace</kbd> even if the text box with the file name is empty. 
1. Enter the new name for your directory.
1. Enter `/` to let GitHub know this should be a new directory.
</details>

Your resulting file should be in `.github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml` and it should look like this:

```yml
name: Stage the app

on: 
  pull_request:
    types: [labeled]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
```

---

I'll respond when you push a commit on this branch.

body:
## What

- Move `TestTracer`, `TestSpan`, and `SpanGraph` from @azure/core-tracing to @azure/test-utils

## Why

1. Having a folder called src/**test**/ does not play nicely with defaults generated by tools such as Yarn (specifically Yarn autoclean)
2. These are test support interfaces, and shouldn't be part of our public API anyway - now that we have @azure/test-utils it's the more appropriate location for them

Resolves #16265 
Resolves #16201
Related #13367 

## Callouts 

There's lots of room for improvement here - we can add a `setTracer` helper, a `supportsTracing` custom matcher, get rid of the duplication between core-tracing and test-utils, and lots of other things that we want to do. What this change does, however, is allow us to make those changes later. This takes care of making the changes we must do before GA - everything else can be punted (because of this)

This is a first step towards e2e tests for redshift, there's still more we should do, but this seemed like a good start. I think the other things could probably be addressed in another pr.

If you'd like to manually test this pr, you'll need to make a redshift config file in `redshift-datasource/provisioning/datasources/redshift.yaml` (I plan to get a test account set up in the plugin provisioning repo so we can more easily symlink this or at least have an example for people, but for now this should work, let me know if you need help setting it up!)

then you can run `yarn run e2e:open` to see the tests run in chrome

To do in another pr (let me know if you can think of more things we should test!)
- [ ] test variables

- [ ] screenshot testing? on the fence on this, but otherwise i think we'll get false passes

* Adds a rust utility class ChildPidWatcher, which uses pidfd and epoll to detect child process death and notify via registered callbacks.
* In IpcData, add an API for notifying that the plugin has exited.
* In thread_preload, register a callback with ChildPidWatcher that uses the new IpcData API.
* Remove shim-side global destructor, so that shadow continues to
  capture all syscalls until the process actually exits.

Fixes #1476

author: jjhembd
body:
I believe code is easier to understand when it is all written in a consistent style. 

For a clear explanation of why a consistent style matters, see Nikolas Zakas' [2012 article](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2012/10/why-coding-style-matters/). Similar arguments are often heard from organizations where software is written and maintained by many different programmers. See the introduction to [Google's style guides](https://google.github.io/styleguide/) for one example.

One tool to help achieve a consistent style is an automatic [linter](https://stackoverflow.blog/2020/07/20/linters-arent-in-your-way-theyre-on-your-side/). For a defense of the use of linters in open-source projects, see this [chapter from the book "The Turing Way"](https://the-turing-way.netlify.app/reproducible-research/code-quality/code-quality-style.html). 

The new module [eslint-config-globeletjs](https://github.com/GlobeletJS/eslint-config-globeletjs) is a first draft style guideline for GlobeletJS modules, written as a configuration for [ESLint](https://eslint.org/). It starts with the "eslint:recommended" rules, and adds a handful of additional rules, most of which are common to many large projects.

This PR 
- Adds eslint and eslint-config-globeletjs as dependencies
- Adds a `lint` script to the package.json to check all code in the `src` directory
- Updates the files in `src` to resolve the problems flagged by ESLint
- Updates the dependencies, so that all GlobeletJS modules used by GlobeletJS are conforming to the eslint-config-globeletjs style

For future pull requests to GlobeletJS, this PR also adds a GitHub Action (based on GitHub's recommended workflow for Node.js) to automatically run `npm test` on every PR that targets the main branch. This will enable reviewers of the pull request to quickly confirm that the coding style of the proposed changes are consistent with the rest of the repository.

author: calinou
body:
`master` version of https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/69959.

This makes distance fade look the same regardless of the camera angle, for all distance fade modes (Pixel Alpha, Pixel Dither, Object Dither). Distance fade now behaves like fog in this regard.

This has a minimal performance cost, but the quality increase is worth it. When viewing a plane that fully covers the screen, I get 215 FPS instead of 218 FPS with Pixel Dither in 4K, but this does not reflect the typical use case of distance fade (which is for LOD purposes). Besides, there are likely other ways to improve dithering efficiency (such as reducing branching or using [interleaved gradient noise](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/50297)).

Thanks to @mrjustaguy for providing the formula here: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/2963#issuecomment-876559516

This can be cherry-picked without conflicts to the `3.x` branch. I tested this PR on the `3.x` branch on both GLES3 and [GLES2](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/50295), and it works as expected there too. This PR can be merged independently of https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/50297 as both can work together.

This closes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/53853 and partially addresses https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/2963.

**Testing project:** [test_distance_fade_circular.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/9407071/test_distance_fade_circular.zip)

## Preview

***Note:** These images should be viewed on a desktop device at 1:1 resolution by clicking them. Otherwise, they will not look as expected due to the nature of dithering.*

author: mbrt-yeah
body:
## Problem statement

If you need to test some data-validation logic, reliable test-data is most of the time hard to come by. Browsing through 100's of pages of data-format standards in order to produce good-quality test data which covers every possible edge case with regards to syntax-idiosyncrasies is also not an option because your day has only 24 hours.

Therefore, it would be great I you could re-use some already existing test-data for testing your data-validation task(s).

This project already contains a huge amount of battle-tested but not reusable test-data for different data-validation tasks in the file `test/validators.js`.

The goal of this PR is to makes the aforementioned test-data reusable.

## Solution

The test-data will be outsourced to a separate package (e.g. [validation-test-data](https://www.npmjs.com/package/validation-test-data)) which can then be imported by every application that needs it.

## Checklist of things done

- [x] Created and published example [validation-test-data](https://www.npmjs.com/package/validation-test-data) package which contains only e-mail test data for now.
- [x] Updated `test/validators.js` in order to pull-in the e-mail test data from the validation-test-data package

## Checklist of things to do

Should the idea presented in this PR find support:

- [ ] Outsource all test-data currently residing in `test/validators.js` to external test-data package
- [ ] Providing documentation for the external test-data package

* **What kind of change does this PR introduce?** (Bug fix, feature, docs update, ...)
Some Github repos have `refs` as their default branch (e.g `v1.3.0`, `2.0.0` etc.). When we try to get the tarball for these refs, Github returns a `300` HTTP status. So instead, make the `ref` as empty to let Github return the default branch (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/reference/repos#download-a-repository-archive-tar).

E.g repos which return 300 status - https://api.github.com/repos/cocos2d/cocos2d-objc/tarball/v3.5.0, https://api.github.com/repos/dargullin/icheck/tarball/1.0.3

No.

This branch introduces grouping of assertions. This is intended to be used to structure assertions in a meaningful way, perhaps to be determined with the work for #110.

New frontend state management code that implements these features use Overmind state machines to manage transitions. To maintain consistency on state management, prior state mutations were refactored to also use state machines.

Additionally, as follow-on work to the repo reorganization, this cleans up the directory structure in `src/web` and introduces an `@asap` namespace for imports.

author: clementmbr
body:
# Description of the issue/feature this PR addresses:

The method [_prepare_stock_moves()](https://github.com/odoo/odoo/blob/14.0/addons/purchase_stock/models/purchase.py#L404) in purchase_stock is here to calculate the new stock.moves to create from a change in PO line's quantity based on its new value and the existing stock.moves, including those actually receiving some products (`incoming_moves`), those returning products to the supplier (`outgoing_moves`) and the "descendants moves" (`move_dests`), which will need at least some quantities to be realized.

The main issue with the actual code is that the moves "returning products to the supplier" are identified by `m.location_dest_id.usage == 'supplier'`... which does not work for returning moves in case of a Purchase Order for a subcontracted product (`m.location_dest_id.usage` will be `internal` for these returning moves in order to manage correctly stock valuation for subcontracted product).

With few lines of code it is possible to override [_get_outgoing_incoming_moves()](https://github.com/odoo/odoo/blob/14.0/addons/purchase_stock/models/purchase.py#L536) in order to add the "returning subcontract moves" to the `outgoing_moves` properly. However these "returning subcontract moves" are still present in both `self.move_ids` (because they are directly related to the PO line) and `self.move_ids.move_dest_ids` (because they are themselves "descendant moves" of the "original reception moves").
As they still have `location_dest_id.usage == 'internal'` and not `supplier`, they will be wrongly caught in `move_dests`.

That's why this PR aims to remove these `self.move_ids` from `move_dests`.
Because the moves directly linked to the PO line are already taken into account by [_get_outgoing_incoming_moves()](https://github.com/odoo/odoo/blob/14.0/addons/purchase_stock/models/purchase.py#L536) and they can lead to errors in case of a return Subcontract move.

# Current behavior before PR:

1. Buy 1 subcontracted product to a subcontractor (`quantity = 1`)
2. Receive this product
3. Return this product
4. Change PO product line to `quantity = 2` instead of 1

Current behavior : The new stock.picking will have a stock.move with product_uom_qty = 1 instead of 2

# Desired behavior after PR is merged:

If this PR is mixed with a proper override of [_get_outgoing_incoming_moves()](https://github.com/odoo/odoo/blob/14.0/addons/purchase_stock/models/purchase.py#L536), the new stock.picking created will have the expected product_uom_qty = 2



--

author: olanti-p
body:
#### Purpose of change
Fixes #648, which occurs when character dies, but there is already a character with the same name in the graveyard.
This may happen when character duplicated due to a bug, or when player repeatedly tries and fails to survive in different worlds and gives their character same name on each attempt.

#### Describe the solution
Create per-character folders inside graveyard. The folders follow the memorial's naming scheme of name + timestamp, thus mitigating possible filename conflicts.

#### Testing
Delete graveyard folder, load a world, die. Character gets moved to a newly created subfolder inside newly created `graveyard` folder.

author: cpu-blanc
body:
Fixes a few issues currently present in NPC trading:

- Fixes not being able to sell items in your right hand, due to a missing `else`.
- Fixes `get_trade_value()` simply returning the global worth and not the trader's worth due to missing returns, resulting in _very_ high sale value, and often far above the buy value, creating an infinite money pit.
- Adjusts NPCs to correctly calculate selling multiple items at once; as once a sale is made, the price changes, and we need to apply the new price to each following item to better simulate loss of demand/the same price decrease as if sold individually.
- Removes a possible exploit by selling items in both hands at the same time, causing them both to be sold at the same rate, then sold back to the NPC for profit.

As a side-effect of this PR, most prices selling to NPCs have been nerfed compared to before. This again was due to the selling price being incorrectly tied to SS13's default worth procs, rather than the individual trader's.

author: raineorshine
body:
When a new thought is created or moved in between two other thoughts, its rank is calculated to be about halfway in between the two. With enough of these operations, the rank can become small enough to run into precision errors. This will eventually cause two thoughts to have the same rank.

On move, check if the ranks are getting too close. If they are, rerank the context from 0...n in whole integers.

author: williamads
body:
#### What is the purpose of this pull request?
Make dependencies explicit.

#### What problem is this solving?
On toolbelt 2.x, our plugins are using implicitly dependencies from the toolbelt. On 3.x, it is not running well, because the way that we are doing is structurally different from 2.x.

When we install a plugin on toolbelt 3.x, using `vtex plugins install [PLUGIN]`, it is installed on `/Users/william/.local/share/vtex/node_modules/@vtex/[PLUGIN]`. To solve the problem of dependencies that the plugin has of toolbelt, a symlink is done from `/Users/william/.config/yarn/global/node_modules/vtex` to `/Users/william/.local/share/vtex/node_modules/vtex`. Diferent of 2.x, in this case the plugin cannot find its implicits dependencies inside of `/Users/william/.local/share/vtex/node_modules/vtex`, because the way that Node.js search, looks only for `path/node_molules` and above “recursively”. Look more about how a require works [here](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/requiring-modules-in-node-js-everything-you-need-to-know-e7fbd119be8/).
Understanding that our plugins on 3.x are not getting dependencies from inside the toolbelt, we have two initial options: Do another symlink of all dependencies from the toolbelt to the plugin, or install all dependencies explicitly. The second option looks better because we will not have problems with different versions in dev or production environment.

#### How should this be manually tested?
Linking this plugin on toolbelt 3.x.

author: joker314
body:
This is a quick fix, and it may be a good idea to follow up with a more long-term solution to validation.

![The input box gets a red border and a piece of text underneath describes the validation issue](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/18113170/124998281-06b73500-e044-11eb-8460-624360f69db4.png)

The above message appears as the user is typing. If the user chooses to submit despite the warning, the input box regains focus (thus scrolling them so that the input box is on screen), the security.txt file is not generated, and an additional red box appears at the top.

![The red box is larger and gives an example of how to format an email address](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/18113170/124998408-48e07680-e044-11eb-8200-bf108ecc0343.png)

The red box does not disappear until the user submits the form again, even after they have corrected all the issues.

**Note**: the validation only checks that the input begins with `https://`, `mailto:` or `tel:`. It does not validate the content afterwards (such as whether there is an `@` if `mailto:` is used) but this can potentially be added in a follow-up PR.

Hello, so I was looking further into your library and found this UTC offtset parsing.
The original line 252 is unreachable code because of line 247
I think that the parsing was intended to do:
+1 = 01:00
+01 = Err
+011 = 01:01
Instead of changing line 247 I suggest simplifying it to always force a 4 digit input for the offset , as even the DICOM standard says "The optional suffix is not considered as a component." - so probably should not be shortened ?
Thanks for considering ! 
It is great to learn Rust from reading your code.

author: jxjj
body: **Problem** Several CI tests related to LDAP were failing as CI didn't seem to be loading config properly from `config/ldap.yml`. When `config/ldap.yml` contained erb like: ``` username: <%= ENV['LDAP_USERNAME'] %>` ``` the embedded ruby wouldn't be replaced with the env variable, but instead would just be a literal string. **Fix** Added a call to `ERB.new` to process the raw `config/ldap.yml` file before handing off to make the LDAP connection. Also: * Added support for loading environment variables from a `.env` file * Fixes failing test re: admin updating URL. (added `expect` statement). Don't want to jinx it, but CI tests were green when I ran them!! 🥳 Putting an image here to record this great moment in history. Closes #35

author: louislefevre
body:
### Purpose
<!-- Explain what this pull request is adding to the project. -->
The PythonShell class can be used to create a new interactive Python process, send commands (Python code) to that process, and then receive the output (including any error messages). This process is accessible globally throughout the entire project, and simply needs to be imported using `requires()`.

### Changes
- Added a new class, `PythonShell` (c509b00d83d47544b9b2bbfc5ae1d82a78931058 & 578df6ec21a426c420b5be665c6cdf708782f83a).
- Added a new dependency, [dedent-js](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dedent-js), for fixing indentation caused by multi-line strings (ca84c77273a414436829d04f71bc115e5affc7c0).
- Renamed `python-shell.js` to `python.js` to be more generalised (79488f7a1b116b7160810a4f3a84724a77d9888a).

### New Requirements
- Any `requires()` statements need to be updated to reflect the renaming of `python-shell.js`.

### Usage
Import the class using the following statement, placing it at the top of the exported Node-RED function.
```node
const shell = require('../../quantum/python').PythonShell;
```

Create an `async` function for the node input listener. All logic which involves the use of `PythonShell` must also go within this asynchronous function, and is assumed in the following examples.
```node
this.on('input', async function(msg) {
});
```

To start the Python shell process, call the `start` or `restart` methods (read the [JSDocs](https://github.com/louislefevre/node-red-contrib-quantum/blob/95cbb7d904288fdbefd815ac4bcb13c03907cfb5/quantum/python.js#L108) for the differences). These methods **only** need to be called at the start of a flow. Note that you **must** use the `await` operator to ensure the logic finishes executing before continuing.
```node
await shell.start();  // or shell.restart();
```

Once the process has been started, commands can be executed. There are a few ways to do so depending on what output you want and how you want to handle it. Again, we **must** use the `await` operator when executing code. Say we have the following string with Python code.
```node
const myPythonCode = `
  a = 10
  for i in range(a):
    print(i)

  print(a + i)
  `;
```

To execute the code without doing anything at all with the output (such as in cases where the output doesn't matter or there is no output, e.g. when importing Python modules), we run `execute()` by itself.
```node
await shell.execute(myPythonCode);
```

To execute the code and return the output as a string, we run the following code. Note that Python errors will also be returned as a string, not as an Error object, so you cannot use try/catch to check if what was returned was an error or a successful output. However, if this proves to be problematic, I can change this so that it will return either a string (if the Python code succeeds) or an Error object (if the Python code fails). Though this shouldn't be a problem because if you do need to check for an error, you can use a callback function (explained next).
```node
let result = await shell.execute(myPythonCode);
```

To run the code and handle the output using a callback function, we pass the callback function to `execute()`. The callback function should have two parameters, where the first represents the error data and the second represents the result data. Using the following code as an example, we execute the Python code in the `myPythonCode` string, and send the output to the callback function. If the Python code caused an error, the `err` parameter will contain the error message and `data` will be null. If the Python code executed successfully, `err` will be null and `data` will contain the result. Note that `data` can return an empty string if the Python code being executed doesn't actually send anything to standard output (e.g. there are no `print()` statements in the Python code). The callback function will then check if `err` is not null (meaning an error occurred), and send the error message to the Node-RED debug console. Otherwise, if no error occurred then we send the result on to the next node via `msg.payload`.
```node
await shell.execute(myPythonCode, (err, data) => {
  if (err) {
    node.error(err);
  } else {
    msg.payload = data;
    node.send(msg);
  }
});
```

Finally, you can also execute an empty command. Doing this is simply the same as executing a blank line in the Python interpreter.
```node
await shell.execute();
```

Some final notes, you must adhere to the requirements of the Python interpreter. What I mean by this is that you must use indentation and line breaks correctly to represent where constructs end. For example, this is valid Python code:
```python
1. a = 10
2. for i in range(a):
3.     print(i)
4.
5. print(a + i)
```

This is not:
```python
1. a = 10
2. for i in range(a):
3.     print(i)
4. print(a + i)
```
The reason for this is that in order to tell the Python interpreter that the construct has ended, you need to provide a blank line. You also need to indent correctly, so any statements within a construct must be indented with at least 1 space. In the second example, the code will break because it *thinks* line 4 is part of the for loop and has not been indented, and will therefore return an `IndentationError`. These rules apply to for loops, while loops, conditionals, etc. Essentially anything within a block.

### Known Issues
- Repeatedly executing a flow before it has finished executing will cause execution to freeze.
- Line breaks cannot be used within Python strings without breaking the command.
- Two flows running concurrently may incorrectly use the same PythonShell instance (needs to be tested).
